claim: Circadian clocks influence many basic homeostatic processes.
source: Circadian clocks serve as internal pacemakers that influence many basic homeostatic processes
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established fact about circadian clocks.

claim: Expression and function of circadian clock components are tightly regulated by intricate networks of feedback loops.
source: consequently, the expression and function of their components are tightly regulated by intricate networks of feedback loops that fine-tune circadian processes
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: The nuclear envelope has emerged as a global gene regulatory machine.
source: In recent decades, the nuclear envelope has emerged as a global gene regulatory machine
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: The role of the nuclear envelope in circadian regulation has not been explored.
source: although its role in circadian regulation has not been explored
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge in the abstract.

claim: MAN1 positively modulates transcription of BMAL1.
source: We report that transcription of the core clock component BMAL1 is positively modulated by the inner nuclear membrane protein MAN1
evidence: This is the main finding reported in the abstract, supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: MAN1 directly binds the BMAL1 promoter.
source: which directly binds the BMAL1 promoter and enhances its transcription
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by ChIP data in Figure 8D.

claim: MAN1 enhances BMAL1 transcription.
source: which directly binds the BMAL1 promoter and enhances its transcription
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by luciferase assays in Figure 6.

claim: Most organisms ranging from cyanobacteria to humans are governed by circadian rhythms.
source: Most organisms, ranging from cyanobacteria to humans, are governed by their circadian rhythms: endogenous and self-sustained oscillations with a period of roughly 24 hr, which manifest in diverse metabolic, physiological, and behavioral processes (Ueda et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: Circadian rhythms are endogenous and self-sustained oscillations with a period of roughly 24 hr.
source: endogenous and self-sustained oscillations with a period of roughly 24 hr, which manifest in diverse metabolic, physiological, and behavioral processes (Ueda et al., 2005)
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: Up to 15% of the organism's genome is regulated in a circadian manner.
source: Up to 15% of the organism's genome is regulated in a circadian manner (Panda et al., 2002; Emery and Reppert, 2004; Zhang and Kay, 2010).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: BMAL1 and CLOCK form heterodimers and regulate gene expression.
source: at the core of which is transcription activators BMAL1 (also known as ARNTL1 or MOP3) and CLOCK, which form heterodimers and regulate gene expression
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the circadian clock mechanism.

claim: PERIODs and CRYPTOCHROMEs bind to CLOCK/BMAL1 and suppress their own transcription.
source: Well-studied examples include the transcription repressors (PERIODs and CRYPTOCRHOMEs) that bind to CLOCK/BMAL1 and suppress their own transcription, thereby forming a feedback loop.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the circadian clock mechanism.

claim: The first mammalian clock gene, CLOCK, was identified and cloned two decades ago.
source: Since the identification and cloning of the first mammalian clock gene, CLOCK, two decades ago (Vitaterna et al., 1994)
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: Mutations in nuclear envelope proteins cause a broad range of inherited diseases.
source: Recently, mutations in nuclear envelope (NE) proteins have been shown to cause a surprisingly broad range of inherited diseases, thus shedding light on roles played by the NE in global regulations at cellular and organismal levels (Padiath et al., 2006; Dauer and Worman, 2009).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: Nuclear envelopathies can impact muscle, nerve, fat metabolism, and bone formation.
source: These diseases (often referred to as nuclear envelopathies or laminopathies) can impact muscle, nerve, fat metabolism, bone formation, and others.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about nuclear envelopathies.

claim: The inner nuclear membrane includes approximately 60 putative transmembrane proteins.
source: The inner nuclear membrane proteins (such as MAN1, LBR, LAP2, etc) include approximately 60 putative transmembrane proteins specifically retained in the inner nuclear membrane and most of them are poorly characterized (Schirmer et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: Gene-rich chromosomes are generally located in more internal nuclear regions.
source: conceived from the observation that gene-rich chromosomes are generally located in more internal nuclear regions, whereas gene-poor chromosomes are relegated to the periphery (Spector, 2003)
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: Gene-poor chromosomes are relegated to the nuclear periphery.
source: whereas gene-poor chromosomes are relegated to the periphery (Spector, 2003)
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: Many NE components harbor DNA-binding domains involved in anchoring chromatin to the periphery.
source: Many NE components such as inner nuclear membrane proteins, nuclear lamina, and the nuclear pore complex, harbor DNA-binding domains that are involved in anchoring chromatin to the periphery (Ulbert et al., 2006; Mekhail and Moazed, 2010).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: The NE can sequester factors that affect gene transcription in both repressive and activating manners.
source: Functional relevance of these positional distinctions became apparent as studies with yeast and flies revealed that the NE can sequester factors that affect gene transcription in both repressive and, surprisingly, activating manners (Akhtar and Gasser, 2007).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: The relationship between the nuclear periphery and the circadian clock has not been probed.
source: Although recent findings highlight the important functions of the nuclear periphery, its relationship with the circadian clock has not been probed.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge.

claim: Lamin B1 plays a role in transcriptional regulation.
source: In order to investigate whether NE proteins are involved in circadian regulation, we began by focusing on lamin B1 since it has been shown to play a role in transcriptional regulation (Hutchison, 2002; Shevelyov et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: Lamin B1 expression oscillates in vivo at both RNA and protein levels in mouse SCN, kidney, and liver.
source: In vivo oscillation of lamin B1 (Lmnb1) expression patterns (both RNA and protein levels) were confirmed using mouse tissues from suprachiasmatic nuclei (SCN), kidney, and liver (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1A and 1B.

claim: PER2 expression patterns are phase delayed in Lmnb1 heterozygous knock out mice compared to wild-type control mice.
source: Oscillating PER2 expression patterns were phase delayed in Lmnb1 heterozygous knock out mice and phase advanced in LMNB1 BAC transgenic mice (overexpression) when compared to wild-type control mice (Figure 1C)
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: PER2 expression patterns are phase advanced in LMNB1 BAC transgenic mice compared to wild-type control mice.
source: Oscillating PER2 expression patterns were phase delayed in Lmnb1 heterozygous knock out mice and phase advanced in LMNB1 BAC transgenic mice (overexpression) when compared to wild-type control mice (Figure 1C)
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The level of lamin B1 can modulate circadian clock.
source: suggesting that the level of lamin B1 can modulate circadian clock
evidence: This is inferred from the phase shift data in PER2 expression patterns.

claim: Neither Lmnb1 heterozygous knock out mice nor LMNB1 BAC transgenic mice demonstrated significant output behavioral change.
source: However, neither Lmnb1 heterozygous knock out mice nor LMNB1 BAC transgenic mice demonstrated significant output behavioral change (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: LBR and MAN1 expression oscillate.
source: We found that LBR and MAN1 expression also oscillate, albeit mildly for MAN1 (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: siRNA-induced reduction of LMNB1, LBR, and MAN1 in U2OS Bmal1-Luc cells results in a longer circadian period.
source: siRNA-induced reduction of LMNB1, LBR, and MAN1 in this cell-based system resulted in a longer circadian period (τ) (Figure 2A)
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Over-expression of LMNB1, LBR, and MAN1 in U2OS Bmal1-Luc cells results in a shorter circadian period.
source: whereas the over-expression of all three led to a shorter τ (Figure 2B)
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Cells transfected with LBR, LMNB1, and MAN1 siRNA lengthened circadian period by 54–69 min compared with control siRNA.
source: Cells transfected with LBR, LMNB1, and MAN1 siRNA lengthened τ by 54–69 min (n ≥ 4, *p < 0.05), when compared with control siRNA (τ = 27.39 ± 0.22 hr, n = 8) (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Overexpression of FLAG-tagged LBR, LMNB1, or MAN1 shortened circadian period by 25.8–37.8 min compared to empty vector controls.
source: On the other hand, overexpression of FLAG-tagged LBR, LMNB1, or MAN1 shortened τ by 25.8–37.8 min (n ≥ 4, *p < 0.05) compared to empty vector controls (τ = 27.7 ± 0.15, Figure 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: NE proteins participate in modulating circadian clock.
source: These changes in τ together with the altered phase of Lmnb1 heterozygous knock out mice and over-expressing mice suggest that these NE proteins participate in modulating circadian clock
evidence: This is inferred from the period and phase changes observed in multiple experiments.

claim: Over-expressing dLamin in circadian neurons with cryGAL4-39 and cryGAL4-16 in vivo resulted in substantially shortened periods of behavioral rhythms in constant darkness compared to GAL4 controls.
source: Consistent with the mammalian data, over-expressing dLamin (dLam) (Padiath et al., 2006) in circadian neurons with cryptochrome (cry)GAL4-39 and cryGAL4-16 (Emery et al., 2000) in vivo resulted in substantially shortened periods of behavioral rhythms in constant darkness compared to GAL4 controls (but not to UASLMNB1/+, Table 1; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Table 1 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Knocking down dLam in circadian neurons lengthened the period.
source: Knocking down dLam in circadian neurons lengthened the period (Table 2; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Table 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Over-expressing dMAN1 and dLBR lengthened the period in flies.
source: On the other hand, over-expressing dMAN1 and dLBR lengthened the period (Table 1; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Table 1 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Knocking down dMAN1 lengthened period in flies.
source: while knocking down dMAN1 also lengthened period (Table 2; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Table 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Most NE protein manipulations reduced the amplitude of behavioral rhythms in flies as indicated by reduced power values.
source: Besides altering the period, most of these manipulations reduced the amplitude of behavioral rhythms as indicated by the reduced power values.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by power values in Tables 1 and 2.

claim: NE proteins participate in the regulation of fly clock.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that NE proteins also participate in the regulation of fly clock.
evidence: This is inferred from the fly behavioral data.

claim: LBR knockdown significantly decreased the transcript level of MAN1 by 15%.
source: Both LBR and LMNB1 knockdown significantly decreased the transcript level of MAN1 (by 15% and 40%, respectively) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: LMNB1 knockdown significantly decreased the transcript level of MAN1 by 40%.
source: Both LBR and LMNB1 knockdown significantly decreased the transcript level of MAN1 (by 15% and 40%, respectively) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: LBR knockdown reduces MAN1 protein level by 54%.
source: The effects of LBR or LMNB1 knockdown on MAN1 expression are even more dramatic at the protein level, with 54% and 44% reductions, respectively (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: LMNB1 knockdown reduces MAN1 protein level by 44%.
source: The effects of LBR or LMNB1 knockdown on MAN1 expression are even more dramatic at the protein level, with 54% and 44% reductions, respectively (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Knockdown of LBR expression reduces the amount of LMNB1 protein by 32%.
source: Moreover, knockdown of LBR expression reduces the amount of LMNB1 protein by 32%
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 3B.

claim: Reduction of LBR expression in fibroblasts of patients harboring a heterozygous LBR mutation results in the abolition of LMNB1 protein.
source: which is consistent with the observation that reduction of LBR expression in the fibroblasts of patients harboring a heterozygous LBR mutation results in the abolition of LMNB1 protein (Gaudy-Marqueste et al., 2010)
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: A decrease in LMNB1 does not significantly affect LBR expression.
source: whereas a decrease in LMNB1 does not significantly affect LBR expression
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: MAN1 knockdown does not change the expression of LBR and LMNB1 at either mRNA or protein level.
source: MAN1 knockdown also does not change the expression of LBR and LMNB1, either at the mRNA or protein level (Figure 3).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 3.

claim: MAN1 is modulated by LBR and LMNB1.
source: These results suggest that MAN1 is modulated by LBR and LMNB1
evidence: This is inferred from the knockdown experiments showing LBR and LMNB1 affect MAN1 but not vice versa.

claim: The effects of LBR and LMNB1 on the clock are at least partially through MAN1.
source: and thus the effects of LBR and LMNB1 on the clock are at least partially through MAN1
evidence: This is inferred from the hierarchical relationship between these proteins.

claim: Only BMAL1 showed a clear difference in mRNA levels when MAN1 was knocked down, with overall mRNA levels down-regulated to half the levels of controls.
source: We examined the circadian oscillation of core clock genes at the mRNA level and found that only BMAL1 showed a clear difference wherein overall mRNA levels were down-regulated to half the levels of controls (Figure 4).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Western blots showed lower expression of BMAL1 when MAN1 was knocked down.
source: Western blots also showed lower expression of BMAL1 when MAN1 was knocked down (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: CLOCK showed no significant change of either transcript or protein levels when MAN1 was knocked down.
source: The non-oscillatory CLOCK showed no significant change of either transcript or protein levels (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The conserved mRNA levels of REV-ERBα and RORα in MAN1 knockdown cells suggest that the reduced BMAL1 expression is not caused by altered transcriptional activation of REV-ERBα or transcriptional repression of RORα.
source: The conserved mRNA levels of REV-ERBα and RORα in MAN1 knockdown cells suggest that the reduced BMAL1 expression is not caused by altered transcriptional activation of REV-ERBα, a BMAL1 repressor, or transcriptional repression of RORα, a BMAL1 activator.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing no change in REV-ERBα and RORα levels.

claim: Cells over-expressing sufficient Bmal1 did not demonstrate period lengthening compared to cells without MAN1 knockdown.
source: whereas cells over-expressing sufficient Bmal1 did not demonstrate period lengthening compared to cells without MAN1 knockdown (Figure 4—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The lengthened period caused by MAN1 deficiency is due to reduction of BMAL1.
source: suggesting that the lengthened period caused by MAN1 deficiency is due to reduction of BMAL1
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue experiment with Bmal1 overexpression.

claim: MAN1 functions to promote BMAL1 expression.
source: Together, these results indicate that MAN1 functions to promote BMAL1 expression, and thus exerting effects on the clock.
evidence: This is inferred from multiple experiments showing MAN1 affects BMAL1 levels and period.

claim: Over-expressing MAN1 in all clock cells in flies using a timeless (tim) GAL4 driver resulted in a significantly increased level of cycle (cyc) mRNA.
source: Consistent with the cell culture data, over-expressing MAN1 in all clock cells in flies using a timeless (tim) GAL4 driver (Emery et al., 1998) resulted in a significantly increased level of cycle (cyc) mRNA, the Drosophila BMAL1 homologue (Rutila et al., 1998; Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The mRNA level of core clock gene tim was significantly elevated when MAN1 was over-expressed in flies.
source: The mRNA level of core clock gene tim was also significantly elevated.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 5A.

claim: Knocking down MAN1 in clock cells did not alter cyc mRNA levels in flies.
source: We also examined the effect of knocking down MAN1 in clock cells but did not observe altered cyc mRNA levels (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: MAN1 knockdown decreased Bmal1-Luc activity by 72%.
source: MAN1 knockdown decreased Bmal1-Luc activity by 72% (Figure 6A)
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Overexpression of FLAG-MAN1 increased the luciferase activity by more than twofold vs cells transfected with empty vector.
source: whereas overexpression of FLAG-MAN1 increased the luciferase activity by more than twofold vs cells transfected with empty vector (Figure 6B)
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Similar results were obtained with a longer, human BMAL1 promoter.
source: Similar results were obtained with a longer, human BMAL1 promoter (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: MAN1 may play a role in circadian regulation by activating the promoter of BMAL1.
source: These data indicate that MAN1 may play a role in circadian regulation by activating the promoter of BMAL1.
evidence: This is inferred from the luciferase reporter assay data.

claim: MAN1 has been shown to exert antagonistic regulatory functions on signal transduction through its binding to R-SMADs.
source: Previously, MAN1 has been shown to exert antagonistic regulatory functions on signal transduction through its binding to R-SMADs (Osada et al., 2003; Raju et al., 2003; Hellemans et al., 2004; Lin et al., 2005; Pan et al., 2005; Cohen et al., 2007)
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: SMAD2 showed significant enhancing effect on BMAL1 transcription.
source: Expressing SMAD1, SMAD5, SMAD8, and SMAD3 had no significant effect on BMAL1 transcription but SMAD2 showed significant enhancing effect, suggesting a possible regulatory function by SMAD2 in BMAL1 regulation (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: MAN1 further augmented the enhancing effect of SMAD2 on BMAL1 in an additive manner.
source: Intriguingly, MAN1 further augmented the enhancing effect of SMAD2 on BMAL1 in an additive manner, indicating that the positive regulatory function of MAN1 and SMAD2 on BMAL1 might be independent of each other (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The positive regulatory function of MAN1 and SMAD2 on BMAL1 might be independent of each other.
source: indicating that the positive regulatory function of MAN1 and SMAD2 on BMAL1 might be independent of each other (Figure 7B)
evidence: This is inferred from the additive effect observed.

claim: The effect of MAN1 on BMAL1 transcription was overshadowed by the presence of either RORα or REV-ERBα.
source: MAN1 increases BMAL1 transcription in the HEK293 luciferase reporter assay but this effect was overshadowed by the presence of either RORα or REV-ERBα, and the impact of RORα and REV-ERBα on BMAL1 was not influenced by the presence of MAN1 (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The impact of RORα and REV-ERBα on BMAL1 was not influenced by the presence of MAN1.
source: and the impact of RORα and REV-ERBα on BMAL1 was not influenced by the presence of MAN1 (Figure 7C)
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The effect of MAN1 was not significantly altered by mutating the RORE sequence in the BMAL1 promoter.
source: In addition, the effect of MAN1 was also not significantly altered by mutating the RORE sequence (+3 ∼ +13 and +39 ∼ +48) in the BMAL1 promoter (Figure 7D), which serves as the DNA binding target of RORα and REV-ERBα.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The effect of MAN1 on BMAL1 transcription is not through the RORE and does not require or impact RORα and REV-ERBα.
source: Together, these data suggest that the effect of MAN1 on BMAL1 transcription is not through the RORE and does not require or impact RORα and REV-ERBα.
evidence: This is inferred from the experiments with RORα, REV-ERBα, and RORE mutations.

claim: A 900 bp region (−795 ∼ +106) was identified to be the region harboring the necessary DNA sequence for the regulatory effect of MAN1 on BMAL1.
source: A series of deletion constructs of the BMAL1 promoter were generated for luciferase assays and a 900 bp region (−795 ∼ +106) was identified to be the region harboring the necessary DNA sequence for the regulatory effect of MAN1 on BMAL1 (Figure 8A, Figure 8—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 8A and Figure 8—figure supplement 1A.

claim: MAN1 has an N-terminal LAP2-Emerin-MAN1 (LEM) domain, two transmembrane segments in the middle, a unique DNA binding domain, and a C-terminal RNA recognition motif (RRM).
source: MAN1 has an N-terminal LAP2-Emerin-MAN1 (LEM) domain, two transmembrane segments in the middle, a unique DNA binding domain, and a C-terminal RNA recognition motif (RRM) that is required for its binding with R-SMADs (Caputo et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: The RRM truncation mutation lost the enhancing effect on the BMAL1 promoter.
source: Intriguingly, the RRM truncation mutation lost the enhancing effect on the BMAL1 promoter (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The DNA binding domain truncation mutation lost the activating effect on BMAL1.
source: The DNA binding domain truncation mutation also lost the activating effect on BMAL1, and this effect can be produced by simply mutating three positively charged amino acids (RKK) at amino acids 709–711 (Figure 8C, Figure 8—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 8C and Figure 8—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The effect of MAN1 on BMAL1 transcription requires potential DNA binding ability of MAN1 as well as interaction with a protein partner through RRM.
source: These results imply that the effect of MAN1 on BMAL1 transcription requires potential DNA binding ability of MAN1 as well as interaction with a protein partner (possibly SMAD2) through RRM.
evidence: This is inferred from the domain deletion experiments.

claim: The region −237 bp to +45 bp from transcriptional start site of BMAL1 was pulled down by MAN1 in ChIP analysis.
source: Chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) analysis revealed that the region −237 bp to +45 bp from transcriptional start site was pulled down by MAN1 indicating a direct interaction (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: MAN1 binds to the BMAL1 promoter region (−237 bp to +45 bp) to enhance its transcription.
source: All together, these data suggest that MAN1 binds to the BMAL1 promoter region (−237 bp to +45 bp) to enhance its transcription.
evidence: This is inferred from the ChIP and luciferase assay data.

claim: Some components of nuclear envelope show daily oscillations.
source: Our studies revealed that some components of nuclear envelope do show daily oscillations, indicating that nuclear envelope is subject to clock control.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by data in Figure 1.

claim: BMAL1 is regulated by MAN1.
source: On the other hand, we found that one of the major transcription activators of the molecular clock, BMAL1, is regulated by one of the nuclear envelope proteins, MAN1.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by multiple experiments throughout the manuscript.

claim: There is reciprocity between the nuclear envelope and the molecular clock.
source: Thus, there is reciprocity between these two global regulatory mechanisms.
evidence: This is inferred from the bidirectional relationship observed.

claim: Lamin B1 is essential for brain development.
source: Lamin B1 is essential for brain development and is required for the integrity of the nuclear lamina (Padiath et al., 2006; Coffinier et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: Lamin B1 is required for the integrity of the nuclear lamina.
source: Lamin B1 is essential for brain development and is required for the integrity of the nuclear lamina (Padiath et al., 2006; Coffinier et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: No abnormality has been reported for the heterozygous Lmnb1 knock out mice.
source: Interestingly, no abnormality has been reported for the heterozygous Lmnb1 knock out mice (Stewart et al., 2007; Coffinier et al., 2011)
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: Heterozygous Lmnb1 knock out mice express 70% of lamin b1.
source: and it is estimated that these heterozygous mice still express 70% of lamin b1 (SG Young, personal communication)
evidence: This is stated based on personal communication.

claim: MAN1 belongs to the inner nuclear membrane LEM protein family.
source: MAN1 belongs to the inner nuclear membrane LEM protein family (Worman, 2006; Bengtsson, 2007).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: LEM domains mediate the interaction with barrier-to-autointegration factor (BAF).
source: LEM domains mediate the interaction with a chromatin-binding protein, barrier-to-autointegration factor (BAF), which has the ability to bind dsDNA, chromatin, histones, lamin binding proteins, and various transcription factors (Liu et al., 2003; Worman, 2006; Bengtsson, 2007).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: BAF has the ability to bind dsDNA, chromatin, histones, lamin binding proteins, and various transcription factors.
source: which has the ability to bind dsDNA, chromatin, histones, lamin binding proteins, and various transcription factors (Liu et al., 2003; Worman, 2006; Bengtsson, 2007)
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: LEM proteins have roles in gene regulation, chromatin organization, regulation of transcription factor activity at the nuclear periphery, and regulation of specific signal pathways.
source: Therefore, LEM proteins have roles in gene regulation, chromatin organization, regulation of transcription factor activity at the nuclear periphery, and regulation of specific signal pathways.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about LEM proteins.

claim: The amino-terminal nucleoplasmic region of MAN1 binds to the nuclear lamins and emerin in addition to BAF.
source: The amino-terminal nucleoplasmic region of MAN1 (including LEM) binds to the nuclear lamins and emerin in addition to BAF.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about MAN1 structure.

claim: The amino-terminal nucleoplasmic region is necessary for efficient localization of MAN1 to the inner nuclear membrane.
source: It is also necessary for efficient localization of MAN1 to the inner nuclear membrane (Mansharamani and Wilson, 2005).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: The first globular domain of MAN1 contains a winged helix which is mainly used for DNA binding and recognition.
source: The first globular domain contains a winged helix (including the sequence RKKMKKVWDR) which is mainly used for DNA binding and recognition.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about MAN1 structure.

claim: The second domain of MAN1 (amino acids 782–911) is an RRM-like protein interaction domain where it can interact with R-SMADs.
source: The second domain (amino acids 782–911) is an RRM-like protein interaction domain where it can interact with R-SMADs.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about MAN1 structure.

claim: The entire carboxy-terminal region of MAN1 was shown to participate in DNA binding.
source: The entire carboxy-terminal region of MAN1 was shown to participate in DNA binding, and this interaction is synergistic to the binding of MAN1 to different transcriptional regulators, including R-SMADs (Osada et al., 2003; Raju et al., 2003; Lin et al., 2005; Pan et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: Both RRM and DNA binding domains are required for the activation of the BMAL1 promoter by MAN1.
source: Consistently, we found that both RRM and DNA binding domains are required for the activation of the BMAL1 promoter by MAN1.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by data in Figure 8B and 8C.

claim: Mutating three of the highly positively charged and conserved amino acids within the winged helix region is sufficient to dampen the activation efficiency of MAN1.
source: Also congruent with previous findings, we found that mutating three of the highly positively charged and conserved amino acids within the winged helix region is sufficient to dampen the activation efficiency of MAN1.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by data in Figure 8C.

claim: MAN1 further augments (but not antagonizes) the positive effect of SMAD2 on BMAL1.
source: In contrast to previous reports, we found that MAN1 further augments (but not antagonizes) the positive effect of SMAD2 on BMAL1.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by data in Figure 7B.

claim: The substitution mutation YV-DD of MAN1 does not influence its effect on BMAL1.
source: Consistent with this result, we also found that the substitution mutation YV-DD of MAN1 does not influence its effect on BMAL1 (though RRM domain is required).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by data in Figure 8B.

claim: The effects of MAN1 and SMAD2 on BMAL1 might not be completely independent to each other.
source: Collectively, these results suggest that the effects of MAN1 and SMAD2 on BMAL1 might not be completely independent to each other
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results with MAN1 and SMAD2.

claim: MAN1 might interact with SMAD2 in more than one way to modulate transcription of target genes.
source: and that MAN1 might interact with SMAD2 in more than one way (presumably through other protein partners) to modulate transcription of target genes.
evidence: This is speculated based on the experimental results.

claim: Approximately 15% of genes are rhythmically regulated by the core molecular clock.
source: Many of our body functions manifest a daily rhythm which is maintained by the rhythmic regulation of approximately 15% of genes by the core molecular clock (Vollmers et al., 2009; Menet et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: Genetic loci associated with the nuclear lamina through large regions of chromatin (lamin associated domains–LADs) are associated with changes in transcriptional status.
